& Schedule Standings Teams MMA Home Boxing Home NFL Week 10 Shelton vs. Fils NFL Projections CFP Projections Fantasy Football Central Play How Portugal’s send-off for Cristiano Ronaldo turned into a horror show
 Portugal's players headed out for the game against Denmark in 'Ronaldo 7' shirts Diogo Cardoso - UEFA/UEFA via Getty Images 
 By Daniel Taylor Nov. 15, 2026 Updated 8:27 am EST Share article 105 One by one, they lined up in the tunnel of the Estadio Municipal de Braga. There was, of course, one notable face missing at the front of the queue. But in another sense, he was still on everyone’s mind — smiling, perhaps, as the night progressed, with a look of unmistakable satisfaction in his eye.
 Advertisement
 This was Braga, in northern Portugal, on the night when one of Europe’s more spectacular stadiums, chiselled into the side of a cliff , provided the backdrop for a series of Cristiano Ronaldo tributes and a result that did more than anything to remind everyone of his absence.
 Portugal 1, Denmark 4 — the scoreline told its own story in Portugal’s first game since he retired from playing for his country. It was, remarkably, the heaviest defeat they have ever suffered in a competitive fixture on their own soil. In 105 years, to be precise.
 Was he watching? In fact, let’s get the awkward question out of the way: was it not a little unusual, to say the least, for this kind of tribute to take place without the subject of all the acclaim being there to see it?
 But the relevant people pressed on regardless to honour the man whose career at international level has reached its endgame, 23 years since it began as an 18-year-old with braces on his teeth and magic in his feet.
 An image of Ronaldo is displayed during the game in Braga (Diogo Cardoso – UEFA/UEFA via Getty Images) Every one of his former team-mates came out wearing a No 7 shirt before the Nations League encounter with Denmark. The mascots did, too (all 23 of them). “Obrigadao Capi7ao” read a huge banner: Thank you Captain. There was a standing ovation in the seventh minute — some fans wore Ronaldo face-masks — as a picture flashed up on the big screen to show his trademark goal celebration.
 Advertisement
 Heck, they had even redesigned Ronaldo’s old shirt number — adding a small horizontal dash through the middle, in the way that many Europeans do — as if the more traditional 7 had to be retired as well. “Time to debut a new 7,” read the explanation from the Portuguese football federation. “Because there’s one that will be eternal.” Thank you Captain, indeed.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Why Portugal can’t retire Cristiano Ronaldo’s shirt
 Now Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his international retirement, what does that mean for his Portugal No 7 shirt?
 Some will think it was over the top. Many believe Ronaldo outstayed his welcome and that it ought to have been easier to part ways once he moved into his 40s, approaching the kind of age when, to quote the ex-British tennis champion Edward Grey, there is usually only real sport left: “It is called hunting for your spectacles.”
 Carlos Forbs wore the new-style No 7 shirt with a tweaked number design (Joao Bravo/Sports Press Photo/Getty Images) Nonetheless, this occasion was always going to warrant something out of the ordinary given that Ronaldo, still leading the line for Al Nassr in the Saudi Pro League, had racked up 234 appearances and 146 goals for his country.
 Let’s be clear: these are mind-boggling numbers. To put it into context, Harry Kane has 126 caps and 92 goals as England’s record appearance-maker and scorer. For Brazil, the five-time world champions, Cafu has the record number of appearances, 142, and Neymar tops the scoring charts with 80 goals, three ahead of some fella by the name of Pele.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal exit may have been messy but he leaves an untouchable legacy
 The forward had a transformative effect on Portugal, the team and the country, even if his ego made him hard to manage
 Lionel Messi, of course, accumulated 126 goals in 208 appearances for Argentina. But the rest are just a speck in Ronaldo’s wing-mirrors. Kylian Mbappe is France’s record scorer with 67 goals, Miroslav Klose managed 71 for Germany and David Villa’s 59 leads the way for Spain, the world champions. As for the United States, it is a tie between Clint Dempsey and Landon Donovan, with 57 goals apiece. Ronaldo hit that number 10 years ago.
 Advertisement
 As the man himself once put it: “There are people out there who hate me and who say I’m arrogant, vain and whatever. That’s all part of my success. I am made to be the best.”

 And so, a walk through Praca da Republica, Braga’s main square, on the afternoon of the match involved seeing more than one Ronaldo lookalike. Closer to the stadium, almost every other Portugal shirt had you-know-who’s name printed on the back. And it felt a little impudent to ask the relevant officials why he was not there to feel the love. “He’s in Saudi Arabia,” was the only pre-match explanation.
 The same question was put to Portugal’s coach. “I don’t know,” said Jorge Jesus. “It’s up to him.”
 Jorge Jesus during the defeat to Denmark (Joao Bravo/Sports Press Photo/Getty Images) As for the football — ah, yes, the football! — it would be an understatement to say that Portugal’s brave new world did not get off to the start they would have wanted. In fact, it would be difficult to imagine how it could have been any worse. “Messi, Messi,” chanted the Danish fans, determined to rub it in.
 Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg, the Denmark captain, opened the scoring with a penalty late in the first half. Rasmus Hojlund added the second and third goals for Denmark with two neatly taken finishes and, when Joachim Andersen made it four on 75 minutes, some loud and piercing whistles could be heard from the home crowd.
 Portugal had not been 4-0 behind in a home game since 1983, when they lost a friendly by that score to Brazil. And it was a Brazilian, Joao Victor, who piled in first on Saturday night. “This is what happens when you don’t respect your role model,” the former Benfica player wrote on Instagram.
 All of which could easily lend itself to a ‘has anyone got Cristiano’s number?’ narrative, especially when Portugal’s new-look forward line — Bruno Fernandes on the left and Pedro Neto on the right, with Joao Felix operating just behind Goncalo Ramos — flickered only sporadically.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Cristiano Ronaldo retires from Portugal: 23 facts for his 23 years of international action
 A selection of facts, stats and pieces of trivia about the superstar's remarkable international career
 Except, of course, Ronaldo was not involved in Portugal’s previous three matches either and, lest it be forgotten, they won all of them, including a 4-2 victory in Denmark last month. So maybe it is better not to make any snap judgments just yet.
 Advertisement
 It is fair to say, however, that it might need a bit of adjustment to get used to the fact that they can no longer call upon one of the greatest goalscorers there has ever been.
 Bernardo Silva, who replaced Ronaldo as captain, made the same point before the game. This was Bernardo’s 116th cap. Yet the Real Madrid midfielder, now 32, admitted it was going to feel strange to take over as the team’s most experienced player.
 “Of course, it is a sad moment,” said Bernardo, who scored Portugal’s consolation goal with virtually the last kick of the match. “Cristiano spent 23 years with the national team. I’ve been here for 12, so I’ve only ever known the national team with him. This day was bound to come sooner or later. But it’s sad for me because it was a source of pride and an honour to have shared the dressing room with him.”
 Portugal captain Bernardo said playing without Ronaldo was a ‘sad moment’ (Miguel Lemos/Soccrates /Getty Images) And afterwards? The players looked shell-shocked as they left the stadium. Jesus was relatively restrained in his press conference, but he did say that, yes, he could understand why the crowd had turned on the team.
 It was also inevitable, as the coach who had dropped and marginalised Ronaldo, that he would be asked if they were missing one man in particular.
 “Missing what?” the 72-year-old replied. “He’s no longer here. He’s missed for his company, but he’s not playing anymore, he’s not here anymore, and he’s already decided his future.”
 Everyone knew the point he was trying to make. It would just have been a lot easier to make that point if his team had not put in an old-fashioned stinker of a performance.
 Portugal, who have fallen two places to seventh in FIFA’s world rankings, had never lost in this manner during all of Ronaldo’s years in the team. Jesus would have known that, too. And Ronaldo, being Ronaldo, it was easy to imagine the five-time Ballon d’Or winner, smiling, taking it all in, reminding himself of his own excellence, maybe even doing a little ‘Siuu’ in his Arabian mansion.
